title: Khadijah hires him
hook: a respected merchant hires him, sees his honesty, and proposes marriage
tomorrow: the black stone on a cloak

segments.voice: Yesterday, amanah, a trust, and a young man the whole town called al-Amin. Your line was be the one they trust. Did you keep your promise exactly? Day eighty-three.

In Mecca there was a businesswoman. Not a merchant's wife, a merchant. Her name was Khadijah. She was widowed, wealthy, respected, from a noble family, and she ran her own trading business, hiring men to carry her goods north with the caravans and sell them in Syria. And like any good boss, she paid attention to reputations. She kept hearing one name. The young man they call al-Amin. Honest. Careful. Doesn't cheat. So she did something that, in the story of Islam, turns out to matter enormously. She sent for him, and offered him a job.
screen: `A MERCHANT, NOT A MERCHANT'S WIFE.` → `SHE HEARS ONE NAME.` → `SHE OFFERS HIM A JOB.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq's biography says she offered him more than she usually paid, and sent her servant Maysarah along on the journey to Syria. He traded her goods and came home with a profit bigger than she'd expected. But what Khadijah heard from Maysarah mattered more than the money: how this young man behaved when no one from home was watching. His honesty. His gentleness. So she made a decision. Through a friend, she asked whether he would marry her. The traditional account says he was about twenty-five, and she about forty; some early reports make her younger. Either way, she was the one who proposed. He accepted, and his uncles arranged the marriage. For the next twenty-five years, until she died, she was his only wife. They had children together: four daughters, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah, and sons who died as little boys. And years later, after she was gone, he still sent gifts to her old friends, and he's reported in Sahih Muslim to have said simply: I was given her love. The Qur'an describes marriage like this, in Pickthall's words: Allah created mates for you that you might find rest in them, “and He ordained between you love and mercy.” Rest, love, mercy. And here's why today's line matters. Before anyone else in the world believed in him, before any angel came to any cave, Khadijah had already seen who he was. She saw him first. Muslims remember her as the first person to accept Islam, and as one of the best women who ever lived.
screen: `MAYSARAH REPORTS HIS CHARACTER.` · `SHE PROPOSES.` · `TWENTY-FIVE YEARS, HIS ONLY WIFE.` · `I WAS GIVEN HER LOVE.` · then, large: `SHE SAW HIM FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who believed in you first. Settle, and breathe. Think back. Before you had proof, before anything worked out, who saw something in you? A teacher who handed you the harder book. A boss who took a chance. A friend who said, you should try. A parent, a partner. Picture their face when they said it. Stay with that for a moment. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them. Then decide how you'll let them know. The bell holds the time.
Khadijah hires him. A widowed merchant sees a young man's honesty, trusts him with her goods, and then asks him to marry her.
Your line: she saw him first. Today, tell the person who believed in you first that you remember. Tomorrow, four tribes, one stone, and one cloak. Day eighty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Khadijah as the Prophet's first wife, the first to accept Islam, and one of the best of women; her marriage is often held up as a model of loyalty and mutual respect.

original.note: Arabic: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, the Prophet's first wife.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Prophet's wife.
what it means: a respected businesswoman who hired him, proposed to him, and believed in him before anyone else.

what a scholar hears: the traditional ages are twenty-five and forty; some early reports put her at twenty-eight. and 'Aishah is reported to have said she was never as jealous of anyone as of Khadijah, whom she never met.
